tagline: Linkin Park's comeback single became the soundtrack to T1's title defense.
headline: Linkin Park's Worlds anthem, with new co-vocalist Emily Armstrong, cast T1 as besieged kings, who then kept their crown.
summary: Released on September 24, 2024 as the second single from From Zero, Heavy Is the Crown was Linkin Park's first collaboration with Riot Games and the Worlds 2024 anthem, sung by new co-vocalist Emily Armstrong alongside Mike Shinoda. Its hand-painted video sent the year's challengers against T1's castle, and on November 2 the band performed it at London's O2 Arena before T1 beat Bilibili Gaming 3–2 for back-to-back titles and Faker's fifth. The song went on to top Billboard's Rock & Alternative Airplay chart, reach No. 14 on the Billboard Global 200 and win iHeartRadio's 2026 Rock Song of the Year, and its video has passed 105 million views.

story.heading: Written for Arcane, rerouted to Worlds
story.body:
The song started life in Piltover, not on the Rift. Alex Seaver (Mako), executive music producer for *Arcane*'s second season, told Nerd Reactor that he met Mike Shinoda at the premiere of the show's first season, where Shinoda became a fan of the series and of its animation studio, Fortiche. Early in work on season two, Riot's music team emailed Shinoda to ask whether he wanted to contribute. He sent back an idea called *Heavy Is the Crown*, and the two worked on it for roughly three years. At a press event at Riot's Los Angeles headquarters, *Arcane* co-creator Christian Linke said Shinoda wrote it with Caitlyn Kiramman in mind: a public figure carrying a family legacy, at a time when Linkin Park were also working out how to carry their own legacy forward.

Then the plan changed. Shinoda invited Seaver, Linke and Riot's head of music to his house without saying why, played them a couple of Linkin Park songs and told them the band was coming back. In Seaver's telling, the group quickly landed on a new idea: what if *Heavy Is the Crown* became the 2024 Worlds anthem? The song split into two versions, a full Linkin Park single for Worlds and a shorter score version for *Arcane*, which later picked up the vocals of the band's new singer.

story.heading: Back from zero
story.body:
Linkin Park had been on hiatus since the death of singer Chester Bennington in 2017. In early September 2024 they announced their return, with former Dead Sara vocalist Emily Armstrong as co-lead singer, Colin Brittain on drums and a new album, *From Zero*, due on November 15. Its first single, *The Emptiness Machine*, was the band's first new music in seven years. The comeback also drew criticism. Rolling Stone reported a backlash over Armstrong's links to the Church of Scientology and her 2021 support for Danny Masterson during his rape case. She responded that she had attended only one hearing, had misjudged him and had withdrawn her support.

League fans had hoped for a collaboration ever since Shinoda was spotted at the *Arcane* premiere, and his love of VALORANT was well known. When the band announced its return, the LoL Esports account replied with what Rolling Stone called a suspicious interaction. Linkin Park premiered *Heavy Is the Crown* live at Hamburg's Barclays Arena on September 22. LoL Esports formally announced it as the anthem on September 23, and the song and video went out on September 24 at 8 a.m. PT, a day before the Play-In Stage opened in Berlin. That evening the band played London's O2 Arena, the venue that would host the Worlds final in November. Shinoda called the song "a real highlight of this new era for us". The video's description even advertised a League of Legends World Champion picture-disc edition of *From Zero* on vinyl.

story.heading: A Meteora-era rager
story.body:
Linkin Park wrote the song with producer Mike Elizondo. Shinoda produced it, Brittain and guitarist Brad Delson co-produced, and Rich Costey mixed it. It was the band's first collaboration with Riot Games. Billboard heard the reunited line-up leaning into its trademark rap-rock attack, with Armstrong's screamed chorus paying tribute to classic Linkin Park, including a nod to the 2007 single *Bleed It Out*. Revolver said the song bursts open with a classic Shinoda rap over a bouncy, *Meteora*-style beat, and that Armstrong recalls Bennington's rasp while adding big screams of her own. Music Feeds found it easy to imagine Bennington singing it.

Fans heard the same thing. Some compared the song to 2003's *Faint*, and PCGamesN reported that people were already calling it Faint 2.0. Its centrepiece is the bridge, where Armstrong holds a scream that PCGamesN clocked at around 15 seconds. Riot's own description pitches the song as a call to every would-be ruler ready to claim the crown.

story.heading: Storming T1's castle
story.body:
The animated video was made with the studio Eddy at Brunch Studio. PCGamesN said its hand-painted look draws on medieval art with a touch of the painter William Turner. It opens on a gold-embroidered banner that scrolls past battle scenes to five figures raising the Summoner's Cup. Then the year's contenders march on a white castle held by T1, the reigning world champions, while Linkin Park perform inside. A rider carries a Bilibili Gaming banner, Brance carries a RED Canids flag at sunrise before returning with Zeri's rifle, and, according to Red Bull, FlyQuest's Massu appears as Varus, complete with his necklace. PCGamesN also spotted G2's Caps and BLG's Bin. Working from a list of references compiled by Shakarez, Red Bull found deeper cuts: lightning that spells out Brance's famous "bot gap" from Worlds 2022, the hug between Gumayusi and Keria after the 2023 title, and a painting of Zeus's 1v4 against Weibo Gaming. ONE Esports said the video pays homage to T1's 3–0 sweep of Weibo in the 2023 final.

T1's Zeus, Oner, Gumayusi and Keria defend the halls, but Faker's grandest entrance is saved for the run-up to the final chorus. The castle doors swing open and he steps out dressed as Azir, which ONE Esports read as an emperor bearing the weight of a long legacy. His famous line "all roads lead to me" then flashes across the screen in Korean. As the song ends, the castle crumbles into ruins around the band.

story.heading: Hit or miss?
story.body:
The reaction was split. ONE Esports noted that the video broke with tradition by putting the band alongside the players. For many longtime players who grew up with Linkin Park, the collaboration was a dream come true, and LCS caster CaptainFlowers rated it one of the best Worlds anthems in years. Others felt the band crowded out the pros, joking that Linkin Park must have won the previous Worlds, given how much screen time they had. Brance's appearance also raised eyebrows, because RED Canids had not qualified. ONE Esports pointed out that these videos go into production months before the season's results are known.

PCGamesN loved the song but argued that the video was caught between a League celebration and a Linkin Park music video, and that its frequent cuts to the band broke the flow of the players' story. It set the choice against the backlash to 2022's *STAR WALKIN'* and the praise for 2023's *GODS*. Even so, the animation itself was widely praised.

story.heading: Climbing the charts
story.body:
*Heavy Is the Crown* became a genuine crossover hit. It reached No. 14 on the Billboard Global 200, No. 18 on the UK Singles Chart and No. 79 on the Billboard Hot 100, and went top three in Austria, Germany and Switzerland. On Billboard's multimetric Hot Hard Rock Songs chart it held at No. 2 behind *The Emptiness Machine*, so the band had the top two places. In January 2025 it climbed to No. 1 on Billboard's Rock & Alternative Airplay chart. It was Linkin Park's seventh No. 1 there and their second with Armstrong. That moved them into sole possession of third place for the most No. 1s in the chart's history, behind only Foo Fighters and Green Day. In March, Forbes reported that its entry into the Alternative Airplay top 10 gave the band 21 top-10 hits on that chart, tying Pearl Jam and Weezer.

The song finished 2025 at No. 5 on Billboard's year-end Rock & Alternative Airplay chart. It has been certified Diamond in Brazil, Platinum in France, Gold in Germany, Canada and Australia, and Silver in the UK.

story.heading: Crowning night at the O2
story.body:
On November 2, 2024, Linkin Park returned to the O2 Arena for the final. The opening ceremony began with Ashnikko singing *Paint the Town Blue* from *Arcane* season two, followed by Tiffany Aris and Mars Atlas with *Still Here*. Linkin Park closed it with *Heavy Is the Crown*, squeezing the show into a world tour that had them at Paris La Défense Arena the next night. The official performance video shows rows of flame and red lasers across the stage and the Summoner's Cup on its plinth. Partway through, the finalists walk out one by one, and Faker is the last player introduced. It ends with T1 and Bilibili Gaming lined up on either side of the trophy.

Then the anthem's story played out for real. BLG won the first game and led 2–1, but T1 took the last two games to win 3–2. It was T1's fifth world title and the first back-to-back championship since the same organization, then SK Telecom T1, won in 2015 and 2016. Faker won his fifth title and was named Finals MVP for the second time, eight years after his first in 2016. According to Esports Charts, the deciding game drew 6.94 million peak viewers, which made it the most-watched match in esports history at the time. Like the castle in the video, the crown stayed with T1.

story.heading: The crown keeps travelling
story.body:
A week after the final, on November 9, *Arcane* season two premiered with an episode titled *Heavy Is the Crown*. The song's score version, sung by Shinoda and Armstrong and written and produced by Shinoda and Seaver, is used in Act 1 as Caitlyn builds her team to take the fight to Zaun. Linke said he liked having two versions with different tones. The Worlds video went on to win a People's Voice award at the 2025 Webby Awards.

The song also found a life beyond games. Linkin Park played it at the UEFA Champions League final kick-off show in Munich on May 31, 2025, alongside *In the End*, *Numb* and *The Emptiness Machine*. A few days later it soundtracked the NHL's promo for the Stanley Cup Final, which debuted during Game 1 between the Florida Panthers and the Edmonton Oilers. WWE named it the official theme of the 2026 Royal Rumble in Riyadh, which Nu Metal Agenda said was the first time WWE had used a Linkin Park song as an event theme. In March 2026 it won Rock Song of the Year at the iHeartRadio Music Awards. Esports Insider's 2025 ranking placed it fourth of the 12 Worlds anthems it rated, the highest of any from the 2020s. By October 2026 the official video had passed 105 million views.

whyItMatters: It was Linkin Park's first collaboration with Riot Games, and it arrived as part of the band's return with new co-vocalist Emily Armstrong after seven years without new music.
It began as a song Mike Shinoda wrote for Arcane's Caitlyn, then became the Worlds anthem as well, so it exists in two official versions, one for the Rift and one for Piltover.
Its video cast T1 as kings defending their castle against the world, and T1 then won back-to-back titles, with Faker taking his fifth world title and second Finals MVP.
The band performed it live at the O2 Arena to open a final that drew 6.94 million peak viewers, then the most-watched match in esports history according to Esports Charts.

It became a real chart hit outside gaming: No. 14 on the Billboard Global 200, No. 1 on Billboard's Rock & Alternative Airplay, a Webby People's Voice award and iHeartRadio's 2026 Rock Song of the Year.
It outgrew Worlds and was later used at the UEFA Champions League final kick-off show, in the NHL's Stanley Cup Final promo and as the theme of WWE's 2026 Royal Rumble.

communityMoments.title: LoL Esports drops a hint
communityMoments.description: When Linkin Park announced their comeback and From Zero, the LoL Esports account replied with what Rolling Stone called a suspicious interaction, fuelling hopes of a Worlds collaboration.

communityMoments.title: Live debut in Hamburg
communityMoments.description: Linkin Park played Heavy Is the Crown for the first time at Hamburg's Barclays Arena, two days before its release, giving fans an early preview of the anthem.

communityMoments.title: Riot makes it official
communityMoments.description: LoL Esports named Linkin Park as the Worlds 2024 anthem artist and set the release for the morning of September 24.

communityMoments.title: Premiere day, then the O2
communityMoments.description: The song and video dropped hours before Linkin Park's comeback show at London's O2 Arena. PCGamesN's writer watched the anthem go live on his way to the gig.

communityMoments.title: The screen-time debate
communityMoments.description: Fans split over a video that gave the band as much space as the players. Some joked that Linkin Park must have won the previous Worlds, while CaptainFlowers rated it one of the best anthems in years.

communityMoments.title: "Faint 2.0"
communityMoments.description: Listeners heard echoes of 2003's Faint and Meteora-era Linkin Park, and the nickname Faint 2.0 caught on.

communityMoments.title: The Easter-egg hunt
communityMoments.description: Working from Shakarez's list, Red Bull highlighted Massu's Varus, Brance's "bot gap" lightning, the Gumayusi–Keria hug, Zeus's 1v4 painting and Faker's "all roads lead to me" line in Korean.

communityMoments.title: Crowning night at the O2
communityMoments.description: Linkin Park closed the Worlds 2024 finals opening ceremony with the anthem as the finalists walked out one by one, with Faker last.

communityMoments.title: The kings keep their crown
communityMoments.description: T1 came back from 1–2 down to beat Bilibili Gaming 3–2 for back-to-back titles, with Faker winning his fifth world title and second Finals MVP.

communityMoments.title: A record audience
communityMoments.description: Esports Charts measured 6.94 million peak viewers during the deciding game, a new record for an esports match.

communityMoments.title: Caitlyn's version
communityMoments.description: Arcane season two opened with an episode titled Heavy Is the Crown, and Christian Linke revealed that Shinoda had originally written the song with Caitlyn in mind.

communityMoments.title: No. 1 on rock radio
communityMoments.description: The song topped Billboard's Rock & Alternative Airplay chart, Linkin Park's seventh No. 1 there and the third-highest total in the chart's history.

communityMoments.title: Webby People's Voice
communityMoments.description: The Worlds music video won the People's Voice award in the Webbys' Media & Entertainment category under Advertising, Media & PR.

communityMoments.title: Champions League kick-off
communityMoments.description: Linkin Park played the anthem in a four-song set at the Munich Football Arena just before Paris Saint-Germain met Inter Milan in the UEFA Champions League final.

communityMoments.title: Stanley Cup Final promo
communityMoments.description: The NHL's promo for the 2025 Stanley Cup Final, starring Linkin Park, debuted during Game 1 between the Florida Panthers and the Edmonton Oilers.

communityMoments.title: Top-ranked anthem of the 2020s
communityMoments.description: Esports Insider ranked Heavy Is the Crown fourth of all Worlds anthems, behind only Warriors, RISE and Legends Never Die.

communityMoments.title: Royal Rumble theme
communityMoments.description: WWE revealed on Monday Night Raw that the song would be the official theme of the 2026 Royal Rumble in Riyadh.

communityMoments.title: Rock Song of the Year
communityMoments.description: Heavy Is the Crown won Rock Song of the Year at the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Awards, ahead of songs by Evanescence, Falling In Reverse, Shinedown and Papa Roach.

keyMoments.label: The embroidered prologue
keyMoments.description: A gold-thread banner bearing the Riot Games sun scrolls down past battle scenes to five figures raising the Summoner's Cup.

keyMoments.label: The challengers march
keyMoments.description: A rider under a Bilibili Gaming banner crosses the hills toward a distant white castle.

keyMoments.label: RED Canids at sunrise
keyMoments.description: Brance carries the RED Canids flag across a clifftop at sunrise, even though his team had not qualified for Worlds 2024.

keyMoments.label: Shinoda's verse
keyMoments.description: Just as the vocals begin, the video cuts to Mike Shinoda in a red scarf, rapping the first verse in the throne room.

keyMoments.label: Brance's Zeri
keyMoments.description: Brance races along the castle bridge as Zeri's rifle crackles with green lightning, a nod to the "bot gap" moment from Worlds 2022 that Red Bull spotted in his scenes.

keyMoments.label: First chorus
keyMoments.description: Emily Armstrong strides down the red-carpeted throne-room stairs as the first chorus lands.

keyMoments.label: The long scream
keyMoments.description: As Armstrong begins the bridge's sustained scream, her animated eyes blaze gold and cracks of golden light spread across the frame.

keyMoments.label: T1 regroups
keyMoments.description: T1's defenders gather at the foot of the throne-room stairs as the challengers close in.

keyMoments.label: The emperor opens the doors
keyMoments.description: Faker, dressed as Azir with a golden bird-headed helm and fur mantle, pushes open the castle doors toward the challengers below.

keyMoments.label: Final chorus
keyMoments.description: Faker stares straight into the camera as the final chorus begins.

keyMoments.label: All roads lead to me
keyMoments.description: A golden sigil with glowing eyes flashes over Faker as his famous line appears in Korean, the reference Red Bull highlighted.

keyMoments.label: Faker roars
keyMoments.description: Faker lets out a battle cry in the closing refrain as the fight for the castle peaks.

keyMoments.label: The band on the candlelit stairs
keyMoments.description: Armstrong stands at the centre of a candlelit staircase with the band around her.

keyMoments.label: Title card
keyMoments.description: The golden Heavy Is the Crown title burns in over the crown on its red cushion.

keyMoments.label: Out of the fog
keyMoments.description: Linkin Park appear as silhouettes in stage fog beneath a glowing emblem as the O2 Arena performance begins.

keyMoments.label: Flames and lasers
keyMoments.description: The stage erupts in red lasers and rows of flame as the band launches into the song.

keyMoments.label: Shinoda up close
keyMoments.description: Mike Shinoda performs at the microphone, bathed in red light.

keyMoments.label: Armstrong takes the lead
keyMoments.description: Emily Armstrong sings under a wash of pink light.

keyMoments.label: The Summoner's Cup
keyMoments.description: The camera finds the Summoner's Cup waiting on its plinth.

keyMoments.label: Faker walks out
keyMoments.description: The finalists are introduced one by one, and Faker is the last to walk out through the corridor of light.

keyMoments.label: The finalists line up
keyMoments.description: T1 and Bilibili Gaming stand on either side of the trophy beneath their team logos as the performance closes.

featuredClip.description: Faker, robed as Azir, throws open the castle doors as the challengers advance, steps out and stares down the camera as the final chorus hits, then a golden sigil flashes his "all roads lead to me" line in Korean.
